paras: The lynching of Fremont Emmons took place at Pawnee City, Nebraska, in the early hours of July 31, 1888, when a mob took Emmons from deputies guarding him in the court house and hanged him from a railroad bridge. Emmons, a hotel cook, was charged with stabbing to death Bertha Schultz, who worked at the same hotel, after she refused to marry him. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and Nebraska papers called this lynching justified while warning against mobs in general.

Emmons was second cook at the Exchange hotel and Schultz its laundry girl; her mother lived near Dubois. According to the Omaha Bee, he proposed, was refused, threatened to kill her and sharpened his pocket knife. On the evening of Thursday, July 26, he met her in a yard beside the hotel and stabbed her in the breast, and she died in about twenty minutes.

Because of public fury, deputies took Emmons to the Gage County jail at Beatrice early on July 27 to keep him from being lynched. Brought back on Monday, July 30, he waived examination before Judge Belding and was bound over to the district court, and the Bee's correspondent wrote that there was "but little fear of lynching now."

That night deputies Liebendorfer and Sullivan, afraid to move Emmons again, hid him on the third floor of the court house. Near midnight, by the Bee's account, about a hundred men from near Dubois, "well organized and armed to the teeth," surrounded the court house square. Finding the jail open, they searched the building and overpowered Emmons and his guards upstairs.

With a rope around his neck he was marched to a railroad trestle over the Burlington & Missouri tracks. A minister called from the crowd prayed, and Emmons then prayed and spoke, blaming drink for his ruin and warning young men against whisky. Told he would otherwise be pushed, he jumped with the rope tied to the bridge, and his neck was broken; many residents watched from a distance, one account said.

The sheriff cut the body down that morning, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of death at the hands of parties unknown. No report of arrests or of any prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage. Street talk in Beatrice, the Daily Express reported, condemned mob violence in general but approved of this act.

The Omaha Bee followed the case from the stabbing, reporting Emmons's removal under the headline "To Prevent Lynching." News of the lynching reached eastern dailies on August 1 in a brief Chicago Times special, while the St. Paul Globe ran its own under "Hemped into Eternity." Out-of-state headlines cast the hanging as swift punishment: "Western Justice" in Michigan, "Summarily Dealt with" in Chicago and "Repented Too Late" in Wisconsin.

Nebraska papers commented directly: the Beatrice Daily Express wrote that "if lynching is ever justifiable there was abundant justification in the Emmons case," though "the mob is dangerous at best." The McCook Tribune ran the story under a headline saying Emmons "Commits Suicide," with a Pawnee City writer reporting that local opinion held the law should have taken its course "but that full justice was done the wretch." In its year-end review the Omaha Bee called Emmons "a bloodthirsty idiot," and no paper gave the race of anyone involved.

Counts of the mob ranged from forty masked men in a Beatrice dispatch to about a hundred in the Bee and about 200 in a Pawnee City dispatch. The hour ranged from about 1 a.m. to "about three o'clock," and a New Mexico brief dated the lynching August 2. The Bee and the Pawnee City dispatch said Emmons admitted the killing, the New Ulm Review said he "neither admitted nor denied it," and a Beatrice dispatch said he had pleaded not guilty. The McCook Tribune said he was lynched "by the people of that city," whereas the New Ulm account said Pawnee citizens "had no hand in the affair."
A Beatrice dispatch dated the stabbing Friday and the Bee's year-end review said Emmons shot her on July 21, but the dispatch written the next morning supports Thursday, July 26.

reader.title: Lynching of Fremont Emmons
bases: A mob of forty to two hundred men took Emmons, charged with murder, from deputies guarding him in the court house and hanged him from a railroad bridge (A5, A28, A22).

Emmons was killed by a mob numbered at 40 to 200 men who overpowered his guards, with no lawful authority, as punishment for the murder he was charged with (A5, A28); the coroner's jury found death at the hands of persons unknown (A28, A32).

Independent specials from Pawnee City and Beatrice to the Omaha Bee, Omaha Herald, St. Paul Globe and McCook Tribune agree on the seizure from officers and the hanging from a railroad bridge (A5, A6, A10, A28).

accounts.label: Omaha Bee Pawnee City special
accounts.gist: About a hundred armed men from near Dubois surrounded the court house before midnight, found Emmons on the third floor about 1 a.m., and hanged him from the C., K. & N. bridge after he said he killed Schultz because she refused his love.

accounts.label: Beatrice dispatch
accounts.gist: Forty masked men entered about 1 a.m., pushed past Deputy Liebendorfer, and hanged Emmons from a bridge over the B. & M. after he acknowledged the crime; he had pleaded not guilty at his hearing.

accounts.label: Pawnee City dispatch (McCook Tribune)
accounts.gist: About 200 men marched in between 2 and 3 a.m., posted guards at the corners of the court house, and hanged Emmons from a Rock Island bridge over the B. & M.; he confessed.

accounts.label: Wire account (New Ulm Review)
accounts.gist: A mob from near Dubois came at 2 a.m.; Emmons blamed whisky and neither admitted nor denied the crime; Pawnee citizens had no hand in it.

accounts.label: Pawnee City, Aug. 1 (Abilene Reflector)
accounts.gist: Emmons maintained he knew nothing of the murder, but in his prayer asked God to forgive him for it.

framing.detail: The Beatrice Daily Express said that 'if lynching is ever justifiable there was abundant justification' here, but that 'the mob is dangerous at best'.
The McCook Tribune headed the story 'By the Rope Route ... Commits Suicide' and printed the Pawnee City view that 'full justice was done the wretch'.
Out-of-state headlines: 'Western Justice. It Is Dealt Out in a Summary Manner in Nebraska', 'Summarily Dealt with', 'Repented Too Late'.
Dailies ran the short Chicago Times special from Omaha or their own Omaha specials ('Hemped into Eternity').
The Omaha Bee's first report, 'Masked Men Lynch Murderer Emmons', described the mob as organized and 'like clockwork'; its year-end review called Emmons 'a bloodthirsty idiot'.

record_check.dossier: No report states the race of Emmons, Schultz or the mob.
One person killed by the mob (Emmons); the other death is the murder of Bertha Schultz he was charged with, not mob violence.
Surrounding the court house, search, seizure from guards, hanging; no pursuit reported.
A mob of about 100 (also 40 or 200) men from near Dubois, assembled for this act; no standing organization named.
Most papers name her Bertha Schultz (Elizabeth in one); times range from about 1 a.m. to 3 a.m.
Charged with stabbing her to death (she died in about twenty minutes) after she refused to marry him; bound over to district court.

info: Early morning of Tuesday, July 31, 1888 (mob arrived near midnight July 30; times given from about 1 a.m. to 3 a.m.)
Taken from the court house at Pawnee City and hanged from a railroad bridge over the Burlington & Missouri tracks in the west part of the city
Fremont Emmons, about 25, second cook at the Exchange hotel, once a Methodist evangelist; race not stated
Charged with stabbing to death Bertha Schultz, laundry girl at the same hotel, on the evening of Thursday, July 26, after she refused to marry him
A mob from near Dubois, the dead girl's home; masked according to some reports
Emmons died of a broken neck; the mob dispersed and left the body hanging
